statements.quote: Unicode separates the character set from its encoding: one abstract code point per character, independent of how many bytes a particular encoding uses to store it.
statements.section: Unicode: One Character Set for All Languages

statements.quote: The idea was broached in 1987 by engineers from Xerox and Apple, the Unicode Consortium was incorporated in January 1991, and the first volume of the standard appeared that October \cite{unicode_history}.

statements.quote: Han characters followed in 1992 \cite{unicode_wiki}.
statements.section: Unicode: One Character Set for All Languages

statements.quote: The code space runs from U+0000 to U+10FFFF, divided into seventeen planes, and is kept code-for-code identical with ISO/IEC 10646 \cite{unicode2022standard}.
statements.section: Unicode: One Character Set for All Languages

statements.quote: The price of universality was a compromise: Han unification merged many Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters that looked alike into single code points, a decision that remains contested because the same character can have different regional glyph forms \cite{unicode_wiki}.
statements.section: Unicode: One Character Set for All Languages

statements.quote: Unicode then had to be written down as bytes, and there was more than one sensible way to do it.
statements.section: Unicode: One Character Set for All Languages

statements.quote: **UTF-8** uses one to four bytes per code point, keeps the 128 ASCII code points as single identical bytes, and marks every continuation byte with the bit pattern `10xxxxxx`, so a reader who lands in the middle of a stream can find the next character boundary without guessing.
statements.section: Unicode: One Character Set for All Languages

statements.quote: The design was made by Ken Thompson, with Rob Pike, on a placemat in a New Jersey diner in September 1992; Pike and Thompson implemented it in Plan 9 within days and presented it at USENIX in January 1993 \cite{pike2003utf8}.

statements.section: Unicode: One Character Set for All Languages

statements.quote: For a language model, this history is not background colour.
statements.section: Tokenization: From Characters to Subwords

statements.quote: A model never sees a glyph; it sees a sequence of integers produced by a tokenizer, and the tokenizer usually begins with bytes.
statements.section: Tokenization: From Characters to Subwords

statements.quote: Byte-level byte-pair encoding, used by GPT-2 and later models, first encodes text as UTF-8 and then merges frequent byte pairs into tokens \cite{gpt2}.
statements.section: Tokenization: From Characters to Subwords

statements.quote: That choice makes the vocabulary independent of any national code page and removes the need for an "unknown character" token: every valid UTF-8 string is representable as bytes, even if a single emoji costs four bytes and several tokens.
statements.section: Tokenization: From Characters to Subwords

statements.quote: It also means that encoding errors travel: a corpus scraped from legacy pages can contain mojibake, a normalisation mismatch can split the same word into different token sequences, and a tokenizer trained on one normal form may misread another.
statements.section: Tokenization: From Characters to Subwords

statements.quote: The chain from Baudot's five bits to a transformer's token IDs is continuous; the model is only the last link.
statements.section: Tokenization: From Characters to Subwords

statements.quote: Sennrich, Haddow and Birch framed the problem as open-vocabulary translation: a fixed word vocabulary cannot cover rare words, compounds, names and morphology, so they encoded rare and unknown words as sequences of subword units using byte-pair encoding (\cite[Sennrich et al., 2016]{sennrich2016bpe}).
statements.section: Tokenization: From Characters to Subwords

statements.quote: SentencePiece extended the idea into a language-independent tokenizer and detokenizer that trains directly from raw sentences, supporting both byte-pair encoding and a unigram language model, and removes the need for language-specific pre-tokenisation (\cite[Kudo and Richardson, 2018]{kudo2018sentencepiece}).

statements.quote: The transformer, the GPU kernel, the data loader, the evaluation harness and the chat interface are all artefacts of an eighty-year chain that grew out of weapons calculations, business data processing, telephone switching, time-sharing and personal computing.

statements.quote: The **Jacquard loom** of 1804 used punched cards to encode a pattern as a chain of binary instructions; **Charles Babbage** borrowed the mechanism explicitly for his unfinished **Analytical Engine** (c.

statements.section: Pre-history: the loom, the engine, and the first algorithm

statements.quote: Lovelace's *Note A* is the founding charter of computing.

statements.quote: She defines her subject: "by the word *operation*, we mean any process which alters the mutual relation of two or more things, be this relation of what kind it may"; she claims the Analytical Engine is "the material expression of any indefinite function of any degree of generality and complexity, such as for instance, $F(x, y, z, \log x, \sin y, x^p, \text{etc.})$"; and she gives the metaphor every textbook echoes — the Analytical Engine "weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves" (\cite[Menabrea & Lovelace 1843, Note A]{menabrea_lovelace1843}).

statements.quote: The earliest *implemented* programming language designed for an electronic computer was **Plankalkül**, written by **Konrad Zuse** between 1942 and 1945 for the Z-series of computers he was building in his parents' apartment in Berlin.

statements.quote: The same manual stakes the claim that, until then, had been thought impossible: "Object programs produced by FORTRAN will be nearly as efficient as those written by good programmers" (\cite[Backus et al. 1957, abstract]{backus1957fortran}).

statements.quote: **John McCarthy** at MIT, looking for a notation that would let a program manipulate *other programs as data*, designed **LISP** (\cite[McCarthy 1960]{mccarthy1960lisp}; \cite[McCarthy 1978]{mccarthy1978history}) in 1958.

statements.quote: McCarthy's 1960 paper opens: "A programming system called LISP (for LISt Processor) has been developed for the IBM 704 computer by the Artificial Intelligence group at M.I.T.

statements.quote: The system was designed to facilitate experiments with a proposed system called the Advice Taker, whereby a machine could be instructed to handle declarative as well as imperative sentences and could exhibit 'common sense' in carrying out its instructions" (\cite[McCarthy 1960, introduction]{mccarthy1960lisp}).

statements.quote: In his 1978 *History of LISP*, McCarthy names the twelve features that made LISP a language rather than a notation: "computing with symbolic expressions rather than numbers, … list structure in the memory of a computer, … selector and constructor operations expressed as functions, composition of functions as a tool for forming more complex functions, the use of conditional expressions for getting branching into function definitions, the recursive use of conditional expressions as a sufficient tool for building computable functions, the use of λ-expressions for naming functions, the representation of LISP programs as LISP data, the conditional expression interpretation of Boolean connectives, the LISP function eval that serves both as a formal definition of the language and as an interpreter, and garbage collection as a means of handling the erasure problem" (\cite[McCarthy 1978, introduction]{mccarthy1978history}).

statements.quote: In January 1960, an international committee of American and European computer scientists met in Paris to design a single, language-independent notation for algorithms.
statements.section: ALGOL 60, BNF, and the two democratisations (1960–1964)

statements.quote: The *Revised Report on the Algorithmic Language ALGOL 60* (\cite[Naur (ed.) 1963]{naur1963algol}) introduced three ideas that have outlived every later change in the language itself: *nested block structure*, *lexical scoping*, and a mathematically precise notation for describing the syntax of a language — the **Backus–Naur form**.
statements.section: ALGOL 60, BNF, and the two democratisations (1960–1964)

statements.quote: ALGOL itself never became commercial, but its descendants — Pascal, C, Java, Python, and almost every modern imperative language — are recognisably ALGOL 60 with different punctuation.
statements.section: ALGOL 60, BNF, and the two democratisations (1960–1964)

statements.quote: **COBOL**, developed under **Grace Hopper** from FLOW-MATIC at Remington Rand, was the first language for *business data processing*; its verbose English-like syntax was a political decision — business managers would not accept a language that looked like mathematics.
statements.section: ALGOL 60, BNF, and the two democratisations (1960–1964)

statements.quote: COBOL dominated commercial data processing for forty years and is still running on the mainframes of the world's banks and airlines.
statements.section: ALGOL 60, BNF, and the two democratisations (1960–1964)

statements.quote: **BASIC**, designed by **John Kemeny** and **Thomas Kurtz** at Dartmouth in 1964, was the first language aimed at *students who were not mathematics majors*; almost every personal computer of the late 1970s and 1980s — the Apple II, the Commodore PET, the IBM PC, the BBC Micro — booted into a BASIC interpreter.

statements.quote: Jean Sammet's 1969 *Programming Languages: History and Fundamentals*, commissioned by IBM to document the field (\cite[Sammet 1969]{sammet1969programming}), is the standard reference for this cohort.

statements.quote: The late 1960s and the early 1970s are when the major paradigms still in use today were first put into working languages.

statements.quote: **Simula 67** (\cite[Dahl & Nygaard 1966]{dahl1966simula}), designed by **Ole-Johan Dahl** and **Kristen Nygaard** at the Norwegian Computing Centre in Oslo, was the first language to support *classes* and *objects*.
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: Simula was originally a simulation language; the object paradigm was an answer to the question of how to model thousands of interacting entities in a single program without drowning the code in nested state.
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: The deeper idea — that a *class* is a type that bundles data with the procedures that operate on it, and that instances of a class can be sent messages to which they respond by executing their own code — was so general that it has since been re-implemented, in slightly different forms, in almost every modern language.
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: **C** (\cite[Ritchie 1993]{ritchie1993c}), developed by **Dennis Ritchie** at Bell Labs between 1969 and 1973, was a very different kind of project.
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: Ritchie himself: "The C programming language was devised in the early 1970s as a system implementation language for the nascent Unix operating system" (\cite[Ritchie 1993, abstract]{ritchie1993c}).

statements.quote: In the body of the paper he pins the timeline more precisely: "C came into being in the years 1969–1973, in parallel with the early development of the Unix operating system; the most creative period occurred during 1972." The chain runs from Martin Richards's **BCPL** through Ken Thompson's **B** ("BCPL squeezed into 8K bytes of memory and filtered through Thompson's brain") to **NB** ("new B") to **C** (\cite[Ritchie 1993]{ritchie1993c}).
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: Thompson had written the original Unix in PDP-7 assembler in 1968–69; by the summer of 1973, Ritchie and his team had rewritten the Unix kernel for the PDP-11 in C (\cite[Ritchie 1993]{ritchie1993c}).

statements.quote: The result is the language in which Unix, then Linux, then the entire open-source stack of the 1990s and 2000s, were written, and the language in which most of the GPU drivers, BLAS implementations, and numerical kernels that an LLM depends on are still written.

statements.quote: **C++** (\cite[Stroustrup 1993]{stroustrup1993cpp}) began life as **"C with Classes"** in 1979, when **Bjarne Stroustrup** started adding Simula-style classes to C at Bell Labs.
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: Stroustrup's own first sentence: "C++ was designed to provide Simula's facilities for program organization together with C's efficiency and flexibility for systems programming.
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: It was intended to deliver that to real projects within half a year of the idea.

statements.quote: It succeeded" (\cite[Stroustrup 1993, abstract]{stroustrup1993cpp}).
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: The design rules he crystallised explain almost everything about C++'s subsequent trajectory: that "user-defined and built-in types should behave the same relative to the language rules and receive the same degree of support from the language and its associated tools"; that a feature "must be provided in an affordable form," where affordable meant affordable on hardware common among developers rather than on a researcher's machine; and that "C++ is just one language in a system and not a complete system," which is why it had to interoperate cleanly with C, Fortran, and assembler (\cite[Stroustrup 1993, §2.4]{stroustrup1993cpp}).
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: The timeline: the first C with Classes technical report was published in April 1980; virtual functions were added in 1983; the name **C++** was coined by Rick Mascitti in December 1983; the *C++ Programming Language* book was published in October 1985, which Stroustrup takes as the birth of the commercial language.
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: Release 2.0 followed in 1989 with multiple inheritance and abstract classes; the **Standard Template Library** was added by Alexander Stepanov and merged into the draft standard in 1994, reaching the ISO standard as C++98; the ANSI/ISO standardisation Stroustrup calls "the explosion in interest and use" began in 1989 and produced the **C++98** standard (\cite[Stroustrup 1993, §6]{stroustrup1993cpp}).
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: C++ has grown, layer by layer, into the language in which most performance-critical modern software (browsers, databases, games, parts of PyTorch and TensorFlow) is still written.

statements.quote: **Smalltalk** (\cite[Goldberg & Robson 1983]{goldberg1983smalltalk}), developed by Alan Kay, Dan Ingalls, and Adele Goldberg at Xerox PARC from the early 1970s, is the purest form of the object-oriented idea: *everything* is an object, even integers, even classes.

statements.quote: Smalltalk came with a complete graphical programming environment, an integrated window system, and a mouse-driven interface — almost the entire personal-computer experience of the 1980s was a Xerox PARC demo, several years late, that Kay and his team had already shipped.
statements.section: Simula, C, Smalltalk, and the paradigms crystallise (1967–1972)

statements.quote: Smalltalk never became mainstream, but the *object model* it codified is the ancestor of Objective-C, Ruby, Python, Java, C#, and every modern language in which a programmer passes an *object* to a function and trusts the function to do the right thing with it.

statements.quote: **Prolog**, designed by Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel, was the first *logic programming language*; a program is a set of logical clauses, and *computation* is the process of finding values that satisfy them.
